Assessment

I inspected all six named files in the public repository at the exact origin-reachable commit 2b8f1ae0ea8c514bd333c45fe11275a2fabfbb81; GitHub reports that SHA as the requested commit and as the main branch head.

One of the three families can satisfy every stated equality and clear the action margins: a static overlapping shared-factor construction.

But explicit covariance does not have decision value beyond the strongest exact relational statistic in that construction. It has value beyond scalar ESS, unary summaries, and the complete frozen pair-count representation. The missing information is a public arity-three incidence motif. A one-scalar typed-wedge statistic separates the pair, and the exact canonical relation graph reproduces the covariance-aware action and utility.

The dynamic linear-Gaussian family and the disjoint cross-time lineage family reduce under their strongest natural formulations: their complete directed-lag or lineage pair summaries already determine the relevant posterior action.

The exact derivation is therefore decisive. A learned experiment would test inductive bias, optimization, or calibration—not whether covariance contains decision information absent from the strongest exact relational representation.

The repository background supports precisely this escalation. Its retained position was that the homogeneous proposal reduced to scalar ESS; its likelihood interface reduced histories to score and information contractions q,J; and it identified a replication-safe relational encoder as the serious alternative rather than a mean/count baseline.

Consequence

This construction establishes:

Structured covariance orientation has decision value beyond scalar ESS and the complete frozen second-order aggregate representation.

It does not establish:

Explicit covariance has decision value beyond the strongest exact relational statistic.

The latter statement is false on this finite construction. The public relation graph already contains the decisive information, and a much weaker arity-three statistic extracts it.

A dynamic collision would require something omitted—unsigned or binned lag, a circular schedule without a boundary, variable unrecorded batch size, or a hidden phase bit. So this family supplies no admissible exact pair.

It also determines the conditional information increment of every genuinely pending remote child.

The relay here is physically valid: it delivers a distinct, not-yet-assimilated child key. I do not reuse the old B1 relay semantics, where RELAY retransmitted the last row under its existing key and ledger quotienting therefore gave it zero new likelihood increment.

Within the disjoint-chain family, identical row and pair summaries imply identical posterior covariance and identical relay/sense/commit risk. Hence there is no admissible pair.

To escape this reduction, a lineage graph must contain overlapping disturbances, forks, merges, or diamonds. But then the missing object is again an arity-three-or-higher incidence motif or the canonical lineage DAG. The strongest exact relational comparator sees that object and reconstructs its action value. This is the temporal analogue of the static wedge, not a separate source of covariance-only decision information.

Strongest evidence against the conclusion

The strongest contrary evidence is the static construction itself. It is not a cosmetic counterexample:

all origins are real, unique, and prospectively generated;

the covariance spectra are exactly equal;

scalar ESS and every frozen typed pair statistic collide;

the opposite actions have a 0.201 normalized margin;

the full-history advantage over any common low-order policy is 0.1005.

Therefore it would be scientifically wrong to conclude that scalar ESS or complete pair-count pooling is sufficient.

The main limitation of my negative conclusion about explicit covariance is different. The wedge statistic is easy to write after the finite construction is known. Across a broad population of unseen factor graphs, explicit covariance algebra may be more compositional, data-efficient, or numerically stable than asking a generic invariant learner to discover all useful higher-order motifs. A containing relational architecture can represent the answer without necessarily learning it under a finite budget.

That would support a possible inductive-bias or optimization advantage, not extra decision information. The distinction matters:

representation contains the action

⇒a finite learner reliably reconstructs it.

The dynamic reduction also depends on exact directed lags and a fixed public batch size; the lineage reduction depends on disjoint one- or two-node blocks. I do not extend either reduction to arbitrary schedules or arbitrary lineage DAGs.

Research decision

The exact analysis already answers the posed mechanism question:

Reject scalar or second-order sufficiency. The eight-origin static pair is an exact counterexample.

Do not attribute the surviving value specifically to explicit covariance. A public arity-three relational statistic and, more generally, the exact invariant relation graph reproduce the action and utility.

Do not run a learned comparison for this decision. Such a result could only distinguish covariance-specific inductive efficiency from relational reconstruction efficiency. It could not overturn the exact fact that the relation representation contains the decision.

Accordingly, there is no result-blind finite population, held-out split, or learned stop rule that is genuinely answer-changing for the present claim. Manufacturing one would turn an already resolved information question into a different finite-optimization question.

The claim ceiling is confined to the stated eight-origin, two-coordinate, one-decision Gaussian shared-factor construction, plus the fixed-batch directed-lag and disjoint-chain reductions above. It says nothing universal about covariance representations, arbitrary graphs, graph-learning limits, communication reliability, changing rosters, skill duration, UAVs, safety, deployment, or end-to-end multi-agent reinforcement learning.
